claims.text: The starting material is an as-deposited nanoscale FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy multilayer produced by RF magnetron sputtering.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases interface density.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases associated interfacial mismatch strains.
Higher interface density and mismatch strain favor interfacial sliding over intralayer dislocation activity.
A shift toward interfacial sliding causes progressively enhanced creep deformation under sustained loading.
Individual layer thickness governs interface density and the magnitude of interfacial mismatch strain.
Lattice-parameter mismatch at interfaces promotes localized interfacial sliding.
Thinner layers accelerate diffusion at interfaces.
Interfacial sliding and accelerated diffusion lead to progressive plastic deformation.
Thicker layers support more robust intralayer dislocation networks.
Intralayer dislocation networks in thicker layers resist creep through conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Thinner-layer multilayers will exhibit higher creep strain rates than thicker-layer multilayers under otherwise identical conditions.
Thinner-layer multilayers will exhibit more pronounced progressive plastic deformation than thicker-layer multilayers.
Dislocation activity will dominate in thicker multilayers and retard creep deformation.
The proposed comparative behavior applies only while the multilayer architecture remains nanoscale.
Outside the nanoscale layer-thickness regime, bulk-like deformation mechanisms may prevail.
The transition thickness between interfacial sliding and dislocation-mediated plasticity may depend on local chemical ordering and lattice distortion.
